title: Build a Thesis and Choose Evidence
subject: rla
passage:
Source A - Expand with Training
A six-month remote-work pilot included 200 employees. Completed projects rose 12 percent and average sick days fell. Seventy-eight percent of participants preferred the flexible schedule. Managers reported some communication delays, so the company recommends training managers and requiring two shared office days before expanding the policy.

Source B - Return to the Office
A department manager argues that remote work should end because employees may become distracted at home and teamwork could weaken. He says face-to-face communication feels more productive and predicts that performance will decline if the policy expands. He provides no productivity data from the pilot and does not compare the pilot group with office-only employees.

questions.explanation: The thesis makes a clear evaluative judgment and previews the evidence/reasoning behind it.
questions.rule: Name the stronger source and the main reasons it is stronger.

options.text: Remote work is obviously the future and everyone should support it.
options.whyWrong: This is opinion-based and does not evaluate the source support.

options.text: Both sources discuss remote work in different ways.
options.whyWrong: This does not judge which argument is better supported.

options.text: Source B is wrong because working from home is convenient.
options.whyWrong: Convenience is not the source-based reason the task requires.

options.text: Source A presents the better-supported argument because it uses measured pilot results and addresses a communication weakness with a specific safeguard.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports a claim that Source A measures productivity?
questions.explanation: Project completion directly measures work output during the policy trial.
questions.rule: Match the evidence to the exact claim you are making.

options.text: Seventy-eight percent preferred the schedule.
options.whyWrong: Preference evidence measures employee response, not productivity.

options.text: Completed projects increased by 12 percent during the six-month pilot.
Managers reported communication delays.
options.whyWrong: That is a limitation, not evidence of increased productivity.

options.text: The company may expand the policy.
options.whyWrong: A recommendation is not measured productivity evidence.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports a claim about employee acceptance?
questions.explanation: The survey directly measures how participants responded to the schedule.
questions.rule: Do not use one statistic to prove a different claim.

options.text: Seventy-eight percent of participants preferred the flexible schedule.
Completed projects rose 12 percent.
options.whyWrong: That measures productivity rather than employee preference.

options.text: Some managers had communication delays.
options.whyWrong: That measures a management challenge.

options.text: Source B predicts distraction.
options.whyWrong: That is an unsupported prediction from the other source.

questions.prompt: Which thesis is too strong for the evidence?
questions.explanation: The pilot supports a limited conclusion; it does not prove a universal result for every employee or setting.

options.text: Source A is better supported because it reports pilot outcomes and proposes a response to communication problems.
options.whyWrong: This stays within the evidence.

options.text: Source B raises concerns, but its prediction of decline is not supported with pilot productivity data.
options.whyWrong: This accurately evaluates a weakness.

options.text: Source A proves that remote work always improves every employee's performance.
Source A provides stronger support, although the pilot does not show that every department will respond the same way.
options.whyWrong: This preserves uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would be weakest in a body paragraph about performance?
questions.explanation: Preference can matter, but it does not directly establish improved performance.
questions.rule: Use the most claim-matched evidence first.

options.text: Completed projects rose 12 percent.
options.whyWrong: This is direct performance evidence.

options.text: The majority of participants preferred the flexible schedule.
Average sick days decreased during the pilot.
options.whyWrong: This is a work-outcome measure, though less direct than project completion.

options.text: Source B provides no pilot performance data for its predicted decline.
options.whyWrong: This directly supports a comparison of evidentiary strength.

questions.prompt: Which thesis best preserves the source qualifier?
questions.explanation: The thesis makes a judgment while keeping the recommendation limited and conditional.
questions.rule: Strong ER writing can be decisive without becoming absolute.

options.text: Source A proves remote work should permanently replace offices.
options.whyWrong: The source recommends expansion with shared office days, not total replacement.

options.text: Remote work might be good, or it might be bad.
options.whyWrong: The thesis avoids making the required evaluative judgment.

options.text: Source B is completely false because it has no statistics.
options.whyWrong: Lack of data weakens support but does not make every concern false.

options.text: Source A offers stronger support for expanding remote work with safeguards, not for assuming the policy will work identically in every department.

questions.prompt: Which quotation would be most useful if the paragraph argues that Source A responds to a weakness?
questions.explanation: The recommendation directly responds to the communication problem Source A acknowledges.
questions.rule: Choose evidence that performs the job your sentence claims it performs.

options.text: Completed projects increased 12 percent.
options.whyWrong: That supports productivity, not the response to communication weakness.

options.text: Remote work is a bad idea for the company.
options.whyWrong: That is Source B's claim, not Source A's response.

options.text: The company recommends manager training and two shared office days before expansion.
Employees may become distracted.
options.whyWrong: That is an unsupported concern from Source B.

questions.prompt: What should a high-quality ER thesis avoid?
questions.explanation: A source-based thesis should be grounded in the provided arguments, not outside preference.
questions.rule: If the thesis could be written without reading the sources, revise it.

options.text: Reasons that come from personal experience instead of the supplied sources.
Naming the stronger argument.
options.whyWrong: A clear judgment is useful.

options.text: Previewing two reasons for the judgment.
options.whyWrong: This helps organize the response.

options.text: Using precise words such as better supported.
options.whyWrong: Precise evaluative language fits the task.

curriculum.learningObjective: Build a Thesis and Choose Evidence
